items.title: 11.2 Domain and Range of a Vector-Valued Function

source_refs.note: Book p. 288: 11.2, the domain of r(t) = f(t) i + g(t) j + h(t) k (every component defined)

blocks.text: The domain of a vector-valued function \(\mathbf{r}(t) = f(t)\hat{i} + g(t)\hat{j} + h(t)\hat{k}\) is the set of all real numbers \(t\) for which every component function \(f(t), g(t)\), and \(h(t)\) is defined.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why "every" component? \(\mathbf{r}(t)\) is one vector made of all its components. If even one component has no value at some \(t\), the vector cannot be written at that \(t\), so that \(t\) is not in the domain.
Each component is an ordinary scalar function, so we use the domain rules from Grade XI. The table below collects the ones met most often.

blocks.caption: Our table: where the usual component functions are defined (n is an integer)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Our illustration: \(\mathbf{r}(t) = \ln t\,\hat{i} + \sqrt{3 - t}\,\hat{j} + \dfrac{1}{t - 2}\hat{k}\).
\(\ln t\) needs \(t > 0\); \(\sqrt{3 - t}\) needs \(t \le 3\); \(\frac{1}{t-2}\) needs \(t \ne 2\). All three together:
\[t \in (0, 2) \cup (2, 3]\]

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Domain of \(\mathbf{r}(t)\) = all real \(t\) for which every component is defined.
2. Find where each component is defined, then keep only the \(t\) that work for all of them.
3. Square root: inside \(\ge 0\); fraction: denominator \(\ne 0\); \(\ln\): inside \(> 0\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Joining the component domains (union) instead of keeping the common part (intersection).
2. Forgetting a component that is defined for all \(t\) is no restriction; it should not be "removed" from the answer.
3. Writing \(\ln t\) as defined for \(t \ge 0\): \(\ln 0\) is not defined.
